utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Today and tomorrow we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Morrison being away for his personal reasons. Yes, before we -- yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Before Mr. Karadzic continues, I would like to inform you that there is one issue that arose from yesterday's re-direct examination that I would like to address in re-cross so -- before the witness is released today. It's brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's about what, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The issue was my question and when I was addressing the children and elderly being held at Batkovic camp and I was asking the witness about it and then Mr. Karadzic picked that issue up in re-direct and the suggestion was that the children and elderly were released. And I would like to address that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Cekic.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, yet again I ask you to speak slowly and, most importantly, let us both pause between questions and answers. Yesterday on page 89 in lines 3 through 8, you said that Batkovic was open to the Red Cross and that they came regularly whenever they wished. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I meant by that was that they came regularly and that no one stopped them from doing so. Once a month they had regular visits; however, like when the prisoners from Srebrenica came, then they would come even every day. When these prisoners would be brought in then the International Red Cross would be informed and they'd come there too. They'd register them and together with us they took care of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the level of the Main Staff, were there any obstacles put in the way of the ICRC and were they stopped from coming to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. I usually had announcements from the commander of the 3rd Corps regarding visits of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How early in advance would such information arrive?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, today for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P5125, could we have that now, please. It's a Prosecution exhibit. P5125. Could this please be zoomed in a bit for the witness and the participants can see the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain what this means, the Main Staff is sending this information to the corps: "We hereby inform you that we approve the following travel permits referring to the visits of the ICRC teams to reception centres." Who gave approval? Which is the body that gave the initial consent and then ultimately the Main Staff was supposed to give their approval?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our case it was the command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the civilian authorities, was there some structure, if you will, that approved such things?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe such a body existed, but they did not contact us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that same page, from 20 to 25, there's a reference to that. Could we now look at 65 ter 4001. Please, I'll read it out if it's very small. "The Main Staff on the 1st of December, 1995." They say the following: "In line with the agreement reached with the CZK," it's probably the Red Cross, "on the 30th of November regarding visits to prisons in territories held by the parties to the conflict and the task of the ICRC to visit all the prisons run by the parties to the conflict in order to register prisoners of war, we hereby inform you that prisons in Republika Srpska will be visited according to the below-specified schedule ..." And that is Tunjice, Vlasenica, Batkovic, Kotorsko, Rogatica, Srbinje, and Mali Logor. Further down it says: "Provide access to the mentioned prisons so that the task would fully be carried out, the one agreed with this commission of the CZK." How does this tally with your own understanding of how this service functioned from the level of the Main Staff down to the ground to the units themselves?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fully fits in. I see here this is the 4th of December, yes -- no, the 14th. It fits in. For example, in Batkovic they arrived on the 5th of September and then after that they came every month and, if necessary, then there were these extra visits. The information I received from the corps was the following: If they did not provide information and if the ICRC would come and visit, I would just inform the commander of the 3rd Corps, stating that they had arrived and that I should freely allow them to enter and carry out their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3242, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday on transcript page 91 from 13 to 16, it was suggested to you that in 1995 civilians were brought to Batkovic, civilians from Srebrenica, and your answer was that all of those who had been taken prisoner during the breakthrough of the lines were brought in and that these were combatants. Did you know what age the persons mobilised by the BH Army were?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know and I do not know how old the persons from the BH Army; however, when they were taken prisoner -- well, it wasn't civilians who were taken prisoner at home. It was soldiers who were taken prisoner, soldiers who started the breakthrough. Now, as I said yesterday, whether there were younger persons or older persons with them who had joined the combatants of the BH Army, that is something I don't know. That is one point. Also, they all came wearing civilian clothing, and at first they claimed that they had not taken part in fighting, that they were civilians, and so on and so forth. However, later on in their statements they did say that they were lined up in units before they started the breakthrough. And, finally, we said to them that we would not take any measures regardless of who did take part and who did not take part. If somebody committed crimes, that would be investigated, but they can freely say who had been a combatant and who had not. So on the basis of that we are going to carry out an exchange, then many of them said that they had been combatants and they said which units they had been members of, and so on and so forth. Because they were afraid, they were afraid that they would not be treated specially and they were afraid of drastic measures; however, when they realised that nothing special would happen then they all said -- they all said whether they were combatants or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was an ordinary prisoner subjected to criminal prosecution?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. An ordinary prisoner -- actually, if there was some suspicion, then police organs, investigation organs, would carry out an investigation. So if somebody became a suspect, then this person would no longer stay at the collection centre, they would be taken to Vanekov Mlin and then that is where the investigation would be carried out. If it would be proven that they had committed crimes, then judicial proceedings would be instituted. However, if it would be proven that he had not committed any crimes then such a person would be returned to the collection centre and would stay on with the other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned statements. What is your experience in terms of these statements when exchanges would be carried out for those who were in Batkovici? What was your experience? The statements they gave to their organs and to their media, to what extent were they correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would object this question. This goes to speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that the witness did have an opportunity to see that because statements of other persons were raised in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I agree with Mr. Zec. Please move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'd like to call up 65 ter 2203. This is the 26th of July. Let us see what the report said about these prisoners who were brought to Batkovic. 65 ter 2203.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the command of the 1st Zvornik Brigade, infantry brigade, is reporting to the Drina Corps? And then here on page 1, paragraph 1, in the middle it says: "In the area of Kozjak a reconnaissance group of the 1st Bircanska Brigade carried out an activity and then they were sent to the prison in Batkovic." How does this fit into your own knowledge? What do you say to that? On the 26th of July people were still being taken prisoner in the woods. As for the prisoners that you received from the fighting around Srebrenica, when was that?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. We received prisoners from Srebrenica all the way up until the end of July, that is to say this information is correct, and it is precisely at this time that I received a group of, say, 30 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, while Judge Lattanzi may be happy with it, but why do we have only French translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that there must be an English version somewhere. The Prosecution prepared this document for use. It is their services that prepared this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We will check if there's English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3243, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now take a look at 4023, that's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us just establish that this is the Zvornik Brigade that is reporting to the command of the Drina Corps; isn't that right? Let us see now what the Drina Corps is reporting to the Main Staff, the same day, the 26th of July, and the Drina Corps is reporting to the Main Staff. This is a regular combat report submitted to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Again, in paragraph 1, last paragraph [as interpreted]: "As for the leftover enemy forces in Srebrenica, during the day 34 persons surrendered and were taken to the Batkovic camp." Is that the same group?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is, 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3244, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, did you notice or did you learn of any planned, intentional commission of evil or violation of laws in relation to prisoners by official persons from the army and state?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During my service, I did not notice that any official committed any crimes against the prisoners. In particular, there were no such cases at the time when I was commander of the collection centre in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information to the effect that there had been violations before you? I'm not talking about individuals. I'm talking about official state structures.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not have any such information, except for what I presented: The attack against the guard and the killing in self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cekic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Cekic. Yesterday we discussed when I asked you about children and elderly being held at Batkovic in 1995, and you said there was no children, perhaps some elderly. This is transcript page 36498 through 99. Then I showed to you several names of the children that were detained at camp Batkovic after the fall of Srebrenica and we looked at Batkovic list which is P03213, and if we could have it on the screen, please. In -- this was in transcript page 36504 through 05. In re-examination Mr. Karadzic asked you about this again, and you said -- and you told us that once elderly and children were identified they were immediately released. They were not exchanged. That's what you told us, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Zec kindly tell us what sort of categorisation he is relying on when proclaiming someone a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm relying what was said in court and transcript page 36508 through 09, and this was during the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you remember this discussion, Mr. Cekic?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Can you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we read out the answer the witness gave. Shall I read out that passage?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When Mr. Karadzic started his re-examination, he asked you to finish what you didn't finish. I will read out that portion of the transcript. This is what Mr. Karadzic said: "Help us, Mr. Cekic, and shed light on some things. You started saying something about the military which captured those combatants including a few who were younger. Can you finish that answer of yours?" And this is what you said, and there's a translation issue whether it was "indictment" or "list": "Yes, in the indictment I saw there was a number of persons in Batkovic aged between 15 and 18 and a number of those who are over 70. Both groups were brought together with those people who were combatants and who were taken as prisoners of war; however, those who imprisoned them, the VRS army, that is, could not separate them from each other. They couldn't know who were combatants irrespective of their age. That's why they were all brought together. A few days later or perhaps a fortnight or 20 days later, we separated a group of some 50 or 60 elderly people. We did not even exchange them because we were absolutely certain they could not be engaged in the BiH army in the future and we released them. We did not even need to exchange them. We allowed them to go to the territory of the Federation; i.e., they went to Tuzla." That is what Mr. Zec is referring to. Please continue, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I -- may I ask only where is there any reference about children, children in the camp? This is simply distorting the overall image through putting such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Zec showed some prisoners under age. I have to check. I leave it to you, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Cekic, yesterday I showed to you several names from this list that you have on the screen in front of you. So we'll go over these same names again. So can we have e-court page 9 and perhaps we can go to the B/C/S only. And on item number -- so item number 136 is Ramo Ahmetovic and he was born in 1924. Can you -- do you see, Mr. Cekic, the last column? What does it say?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And what does it say?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Hakija Ahmetovic -- no, Ramo Ahmetovic, son of Selvo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the last column for him says what? Does it say "exchanged" ?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last column, "exchanged," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have now -- can we now have e-court page 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Item number 29 is Haris Dzenanovic born in 1978, 17 at the time. For him in the last column it says "exchanged," does it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Item number 31 is Mirsad Dzanic, born in 1980, 15 at the time. For him it says "exchanged," does it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have e-court page 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Item number 223 is Nermin Hakic, born in 1980. For him it says "exchanged," does it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The number is 223, but I believe for all of -- except maybe one. The item number is 223. It says "exchanged."

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we go --

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is in dispute here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I just want to point out the same issue is that what I showed yesterday, e-court page 131, item number 191, Hazim Mujanovic born in 1980, again "exchanged." So the issue, Mr. Cekic, is these children and elderly persons that we saw, they were exchanged and not - as you were suggesting here to us - that they were just released. So that's the issue. So now you can see they were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I reply? It is correct. On this list we registered that everyone was exchanged. Those who were not exchanged, i.e., who were released before that, were the older people born before 1930. Now, as for what the Presiding Judge said and what I mentioned yesterday, they were not exchanged but released. However, they were registered here as having been exchanged. We did not have any other or different kind of treatment for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I showed you person 12 years older than you, Ramo Ahmetovic born in 1926, exchanged. I can show to you other people who were released and it says "released." For these people there is no mistake, they were exchanged, not released. That's the issue and that's what happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, is Mr. Zec testifying or is he asking a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he was asking a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't see any question in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question mark is missing from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think there's a good reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: What I just told you, Mr. Cekic, that was correct at the time, not what you suggested to us today?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened as I said yesterday and as I'm saying today. I don't know what your estimate of it is, but I'm telling you about how things happened on the spot and that is true no matter what some document says. There were some elderly who could not be exchanged simply because they were elderly. We could not have them exchanged for fighters. We released them for that and some of them were even infirm. Now, whether the clerk registered them as having been released or exchanged, that is less important. I'm telling you how things were and you can do what you like with it. As for these younger people, they were not children. To me, children are small. There were no small children there. A boy of 17 who is physically strong and who's bigger than me, that is true, he is not of age but he is fully capable of fighting. That person was also exchanged. So such younger persons were exchanged; however, the elderly were not, only some of them. But some 50 of them were released without having been exchanged. I don't see what's in dispute in whether a person was released or exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This list does not reflect 50 elderly people being released --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: But perhaps this is, Your Honours, for you to look at the list later on. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could -- just could you remind the meaning of the second- and third-last column, the dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can upload the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we have English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We don't have maybe for this list of names but [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we upload the English. Just a second. Yes, date and time of arrival in collection centre and the date and time of departure from the collection centre. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, can I be given an opportunity to shed some light on what was addressed in re-cross?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly what it is that you wanted to shed light on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, what's on page 12. The witness said "all for all," but it was not well understood. I wanted to shed some light. Did he mean an exchange all for all when he said "all were exchanged." That's one thing. Another thing, let's look at some years of birth that are on the first page of the English version so as to be able to ask how those people were released. For example, the person in question was 33 -- no, 35. And I can also see on page 78 that a few escaped, that is, 78 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow about 33, 35.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thirty-five years of age - page 1, item 15 in the English - that person was born in 1960 and was released for some reason and not exchanged. On page 78 there are two or three who escaped. Alihodzic, released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the -- Mr. Zec's point whether the elderly were released as he indicated during the re-examination. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, before you render your decision. The witness said that the year of birth was not the criterion, but the physical look and agility. To corroborate that, we see this man of 35 who was released. Obviously it was assessed that he was unable to fight. That's what I wanted to ask the witness, what did he mean when he said that the year of birth was not the decisive criterion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may make submissions on that issue, but the Chamber is of the view that those points you raised do not arise from the re-cross-examination of Mr. Zec. So we'll conclude this witness's evidence. Mr. Cekic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if -- could the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope to be able to reconcile the two facts that we have a king here, because that's what your last name stands for, and a president. For starters, I would kindly ask you to utter our sentences slowly and pause between question and answer so as to have everything recorded. Mr. Kralj, did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did talk to the Defence team and I provided a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Defence submitted your testimony in -- that your testimony was offered in lieu of leading you live now, your testimony from another case?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, during that conversation it was offered to me that my earlier testimony in another case be tendered instead of my statement and I agreed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The answers you provided in the Popovic case during your testimony, if you were put the same questions today would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: My answers would be identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I seek to tender the testimony in question and the attached documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have offered 69 associated exhibits with this testimony and none of them were on our 65 ter list because the witness was added after that list was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Last night during the course of -- I'm sorry, yesterday I asked my -- our Chamber staff to convey the message of the Chamber to the parties that certain documents do not form part of -- indispensable or inseparable part of the statement. They are 1D7262, I will omit 1 D, 7264, 7271, 7277, 7279, 7283, 7287, 7288, 7292, and 7293. Further, among the associated exhibits additionally tendered in an updated list, updated notice, the Chamber is of the view that 1D7310, 7313, and 7314 do not form an indispensable and inseparable -- or inseparable part of the statement. So therefore, if Mr. Karadzic wants to tender those documents, he needs to lead them live. I'd like to hear from you, Ms. Edgerton, whether you have any objection otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No, I have no objection otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So except for those documents I referred to, Mr. Kralj's testimony as well as other associated exhibits will be admitted with the caveat as regards four intercepts; that is, 1D7260, 7263, 7265, and 7266. Where the witness is not one of the interlocutors, they will be marked for identification. So shall we give the number for the testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 65 ter number 1D7206 will be Exhibit D3245.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And all the other associated exhibits will be given numbers in due course by the Registrar. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Dr. Karadzic will lead a few of those live as well as some additional documents and just for the notice of the Prosecution those three that were on our supplemental list, if they want to lead them they can do that but we won't be doing that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I would like to read Mr. Slavko Kralj's statement, or rather, a summary thereof in English and then I would lead a few documents live. [In English] Slavko Kralj was a JNA officer who served in a United Nations peacekeeping mission on the Iran-Iraq border in 1989. When the war broke out in Bosnia in 1992, he joined the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS, where he served as a liaison officer. He remained in that position until November 1994 when he was assigned to the VRS Main Staff in the department for communication with international military representatives. At that time, Mr. Kralj held the rank of major. He was promoted to lieutenant-colonel in mid-1995. His duties in the Main Staff were to acquaint himself with all procedures relating to co-operation with UNPROFOR and other international organisations and to assist his immediate superior, Colonel Milos Djurdjic, in his work with these organisations and in his absence to be able to prepare the required documents and to be able to submit them for processing according to the previously established procedure. Approval of the passage of UNPROFOR military convoys was placed in the hands of the army, while the approval of the passage of humanitarian aid convoys was in the hands of a co-ordinating body attached to the Government of Republika Srpska in Pale and headed by Vice-President Nikola Koljevic. Colonel Djurdjic was a member of that co-ordinating body. They received information that the convoys sometimes contained military equipment destined for the enemy and that certain humanitarian organisations were engaged in intelligence-gathering activities. During the war, the VRS had considerable difficulties convincing the civilian population that the humanitarian convoys should pass, because members of the population believed they were not receiving sufficient aid while the other side was receiving too much aid. There were some incidents at check-points caused by civilians who held this attitude. All of the military organs of power from the president and the president of the Assembly took the position that the convoys of humanitarian aid should be allowed to pass to the other side without obstruction. The procedure for UNPROFOR convoys in 1995 was that the convoy would be announced at least 48 hours in advance. His office would receive the request and process it for approval to the general -- of General Mladic or General Milovanovic. They would signify their approval by placing their initials on the document. If some items were not approved, it would be noted on the document. The document would then be faxed to UNPROFOR as well as to the check-points in the field. The Main Staff's policy was to allow supplies for the enclaves that were truly needed. There was no change of policy towards the enclaves in 1995. He was not familiar with the part of directive 7 which referred to reducing the supplies to the enclaves. In early 1995 the VRS had intelligence that UNPROFOR was sharing some of the fuel it brought in Srebrenica -- into Srebrenica with the BH Army. The VRS also had information that part of humanitarian aid was being delivered to the BH Army in the enclaves. That was one of the reasons why they had to check the convoys. There was a Swedish project in Srebrenica and in 1994 and 1995, the VRS allowed building materials to enter Srebrenica for that project. After the NATO air strikes in May 1995, there was a period of time when convoys were suspended at the direction of UNPROFOR. And that would be the summary of testimony that is admitted instead of live testimony. Now I would like to ask Mr. Kralj several questions and show several documents and Mr. Kralj is also excellent in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, the information on illegal materials, materiel, ammunition, and other war assets that were found in the convoys, was that information correct according to what you in the Main Staff learned from the ground?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, all the information that the Main Staff received was correct. The information that concerned the convoys and the abuse of humanitarian aid convoys headed for the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up 1D7323 in e-court. Mr. Kralj, please help us and tell us whether this is a report by the Rogatica Brigade pertaining to the 8th of May, 1994. The report is about the convoy. Please take your time and read the first page.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: This is a report --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't have to read this aloud, Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of the page you will see that it says that the convoy was stopped and you will see why it was stopped. It says here we explained to them in a civilised way that there was a problem with the cargo, that we had to inform the Main Staff, but that we hoped a swift solution would be found. They reciprocated our fairness by telling us that they understood the situation. Then it says there were consultations with the Main Staff. Can we go to the following page now in English as well. You see here in the middle they looked for bread. They offered us 20 marks. They got the bread but without payment. And then we see that the back of the convoy moved in an authorised manner, the leader of the convoy addressed the Canadians, and they said -- then he said they had messed up completely, that they had made a few mistakes. Can you see that? Towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page. Do you see here which illegal items were transported, a radio set, antenna satellites, navigation devices? Can you please tell us -- lasers. Can you tell us, please, why did the Army of Republika Srpska felt so sensitive to the transport of such assets in the direction of the enemy's side? What were these assets used for?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, it took some time for us to get to a question, actually. I think that Dr. Karadzic could have asked the question without reading in the whole document or large parts of the document and effectively leading the witness to the answer. And there's not been a single foundational question with regard to this document. Does the witness recognise it? Has the witness had an opportunity to see it? Did he see it at the time? Is it the sort of document he would, in the course of his work with the Main Staff or elsewhere within the 1st Krajina Corps, have received? Did he actually receive it at that time? These are the questions that Dr. Karadzic, in my submission, should be asking the witness before the question that we've just received, which was: Why did the Army of Republika Srpska feel sensitive with respect to the transport of assets? Rather than have the document read to the witness. That's leading and it's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think you need to respond to that. You must appreciate Ms. Edgerton's submission. Why don't you reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Excellency. I asked the gentleman whether the information from the ground was correct, the information that reached them. I'm not interested in whether he saw every document. Five or six documents arrived from the same check-points at different times. I'm not asking about the document. I'm asking about the materiel and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, why would you say that this document is part of the information that arrived from the ground? What were the reasons for the Army of Republika Srpska to ban the transport of such loads, of such cargos?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Army of Republika Srpska did not allow people to bring equipment and assets into the enclave if we knew that they would be used by the Muslim army. This is a blatant example of such assets which were exclusively intended for the Muslim army in the enclave. We were informed about that by our operations organs. They forwarded such documents to us if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On what basis?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness was called to testify to the kind of procedure that was in place for the convoys. It says in the indictment that I, my services, or my army obstructed those convoys for reasons which were not militarily justified, i.e., for criminal reasons. I would like to use this witness to shed some light on those reasons. Were there enough reasons for the Army of Republika Srpska to put a halt to some of those convoys? We heard a representative of an international organisation who said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- they had very few problems in view of the fact that there was over 700 such vehicles moving around Republika Srpska on a daily basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There should be no problem with you leading the witness to that effect, but what did you ask the witness about this document? What did the witness say about this document? That's the point Ms. Edgerton raised. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The witness did say that this was an example of -- consistent with what he had said both in his testimony, and that part of the testimony is at page 293 -- excuse me, 29238 and 29241 of the transcript from Popovic, in which he said that they had received information that convoys sometimes contained military equipment destined for the enemy and that certain humanitarian organisations were engaged in intelligence-gathering activities. And so this witness at page 23, line 23, basically said that this is an example of -- and consistent with what he had said in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When I asked Mr. Karadzic to reformulate his question after having heard Ms. Edgerton's objection, he didn't put some proper questions because it was read out, it was a very much leading question. So I expected some foundational question. But in this case we'll admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3302, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I have a few documents from the same check-points. They were issued at different times. I don't know what the position of the Chamber is with this regard. May I, for example, be allowed to call up 1D7262? That document was issued a year later and the Trial Chamber was of the opinion that this should be led live, 1D7262. And while we are waiting, Mr. Kralj, let me ask you this: How often, if at all, were there cargos which were not admissible? Were these exceptions? How often did you receive information to the effect that those things were happening at one of the check-points?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, the check-points had the following obligation. Through the brigade reports they were supposed to say what the situation was regarding the passage of convoys. As concerns regular convoy passage, there weren't particular explanations provided except that such and such a convoy passed through. And if something happened that had not been authorised or allowed, then that would be additionally explained in a document regarding that particular matter. There were such incidents, but it didn't happen all the time and it didn't happen excessively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says here in paragraph 3: "The UNHCR convoy from Karakaj to Zepa which arrived at the check-point yesterday is still at Rogatica undergoing a detailed search since yesterday ammunition for infantry weapons was found." Can you tell us the following: Did you establish that anyone kept a convoy that was totally regular? I'm sorry, it's the same check-point but it's just a year later.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, all check-points had orders and instructions to search convoys. If there was no problem, then they should be allowed to pass in a civilised way and they could head to the enclaves. However, if there were problems, if there were goods that were not allowed there, they should be seized or consultations should be carried out with the superior command. And the convoys should be allowed to pass. If there was a major problem, like a problem with ammunition, then such a convoy would be kept there until the matter was resolved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this may be a good example. You could have put question before showing this passage to the witness. After showing this passage, if you ask a question, that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll do my best, Excellency, to act accordingly. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3303, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the position of the Main Staff was as regards these obstacles that were put there by disgruntled civilians or did the Main Staff do the contrary, try to persuade people to let convoys pass?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, the position of the Main Staff was that any kind of misunderstandings with convoys should be avoided, or with UNPROFOR for that matter. So to that end, they sent military police escorts and sometimes even the civilian police would provide an escort so that convoys with humanitarian aid could safely pass through the territory of Republika Srpska. Personally, on several occasions, I escorted convoys of the UNHCR with the civilian police and military police from Gradiska through Banja Luka, to Turbe. At the time there were disgruntled civilians and refugees and also persons on the separation line complained. However, I provided explanations and also commanders of -- commanders also provided explanations so the convoys would invariably cross over to the other side safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1317, could we please have that now -- 7317.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was suggested here in the indictment issued against me and the evidence presented that these were not spontaneous obstacles, rather, that this had been staged. What is your knowledge? Did the army pretend and did they take advantage of the population in order to stop convoys?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was in the convoy business from 1992. I'm not aware of a single case when the army pretended to do anything to stop the passage of the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, please go on.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: On the contrary, what was done was the exact opposite. Everything was done to enable the passage of convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please focus on this information provided by General Mladic end of November 1992. You see here on the first page that he is describing a convoy going to Srebrenica, 16 vehicles, in Bratunac, three vehicles, and he says that people were angry and that there were irregularities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here on the second page: "Through the engagement of the Republika Srpska Army Main Staff and the Drina Corps as well as the influence of the President of the Presidency, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, and the authorities, the citizens of the above places understood the situation, and after inspection the convoy passed and arrived in Srebrenica unimpeded." And it says: "The Muslim extremists' attempt to use the rightful wrath of the Serbian people against the injustice manifested through preventing the passage of the convoy and the refusal of the Bratunac citizens to accept humanitarian aid ...," et cetera. This attempt failed. How does this tally with your own knowledge concerning the position of the Main Staff and the Presidency of the republic, in terms of persuading people not to hinder convoys and the UNHCR in any way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The representatives of the Main Staff, whenever they stayed in the areas that that were in charge of explained to the representatives of the authorities the need for convoys to pass, that this was an obligation that had been undertaken. And in a later stage there were agreements to the effect that part of the aid would go to Republika Srpska as well. This had a positive influence on matters in terms of convoy passage, especially when expellees and refugees in Republika Srpska really needed this aid and when it reached them. Then it was easier for convoys to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3304, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the position of commands with regard to robbery and other unfair or improper treatment of members of UNPROFOR or other international organisations in the field? What was the position and what was the attitude of the Main Staff and the second command with regard to this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska issued an order stating exactly what check-points were supposed to look like, emphasising the selection of personnel and equipment and also the need for units in their own areas of responsibility to take all necessary measures in order to prevent possible incidents or have their number reduced to a minimum. The Main Staff wished at all costs to avoid any kind of incidents with UNPROFOR or humanitarian organisations. Muslim forces, on the contrary, carried out propaganda activities and wanted incidents to happen to a large extent which would lead to NATO intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at 65 ter 19054.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on 053 from the Main Staff and this is from the Drina Corps. This is further elaboration. The text is basically the same. And now in the introduction it says that UNPROFOR's mandate was verified by the Assembly. And it says further on that there are certain hindrances, and regardless of our objections, they should be allowed to carry out their mission of peace. Then you see what it says further on, this irregular conduct carried out by masked persons, armed persons, who were seizing vehicles, and so on and so forth. Please familiarise yourself with this text. This text is from 1995 and the one we saw a moment ago was from 1992. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber about this document and these orders -- actually, can we have the next page, or rather, the bottom of this page first in Serbian and then the next page both in Serbian and in English. So you did see this introduction, didn't you? Robbery, attacks, crimes, you see what it says there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I do, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And here an order is issued to commanders of units to make use of all available forces, to investigate and carry out all other activities and pre-trial procedure. The military police will do their job. How does this tally with your own knowledge about the position of official organs regarding such irregular conduct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have to bear in mind that there was a war going on and that there was small groups there that had interests of their own, to rob things, seize things and in this way major damage would be inflicted on the Army of Republika Srpska. So everyone, especially in the domain of command, took appropriate measures for this not to happen. Such persons were searched for and eliminated from areas where convoys would pass, if they would appear in these areas. Also, appropriate legal measures were taken. I haven't got any concrete examples as to who these persons were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go back to page 1 just to establish what the number is. And let us see whether this is some kind of propaganda material or is this strictly confidential material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is an official document. It is marked "strictly confidential" and by no means can this be propaganda material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, 65 ter 19053, 54 is from the Main Staff, and 55 and from the Bircanska Brigade. And from the sequence we can see how this order is further elaborated towards the fields and I would like to tender all of these documents into evidence. The wording is basically the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we see 19053?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be called up? I think it was on that list -- no, it wasn't on the list. Could it please be called up?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if there's going to be a question about these documents, could Dr. Karadzic please be reminded not to lead the witness to his answers. This last document again had huge paragraphs read out to the witness before Dr. Karadzic asked the question which actually could have proceeded any reference to the document and quite effectively.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope it wasn't so. I hope I asked what in his knowledge was the position of the Main Staff vis-a-vis criminal behaviour as regards UNPROFOR and the convoys and international organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Indeed he asked about the robbery, but in a very general way. Let's continue. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this is not the document. 1D -- actually, 65 ter 19053. I don't think this is the document. In the meantime, can we have 1D19055 while we're waiting for 053.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1D9055.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's a good time to take a break. We'll break for half an hour and resume at three past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I owe you an apology. 19053 has already been admitted as a P exhibit and I'd like to have next 19055, which is a further elaboration of the previous two documents. Just before that, could we have 19054 admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3305, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the document I asked for. I would like to have 19055.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think this is 19055.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something different, the Ministry of the Interior -- no, no. I'll drop that. 1905 [as interpreted], I thought it was something else, must have been a mistake. In any case, we'll drop this document. For the participants, 19053 has been admitted as P2247, it's the same wording, the same subject matter. It's just that it came from the Main Staff to the corps command and the brigade command. The other one is 19050, can we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, please have a look and tell us if this is the same document we saw a moment ago sent to the Bircani Brigade. What corps did the Bircani Brigade belong to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Bircani Brigade was in the Drina Corps and this is the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 2 so as to see who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the colonel in command of the Bircani Brigade at the time? Can we have the next page in Serbian too.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2 in the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is a one-page document in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: English has item 4 and 5 in its order we see on -- item 3 -- second page seems to be missing, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it wasn't uploaded. It does exist, though, and I would kindly ask that it be uploaded. I believe it says Colonel Svetozar Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it ring a bell? Lieutenant-Colonel, is the name familiar to you? Could it have been Andric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Andric was the commander of that brigade. I recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Second page must be located and uploaded. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3306, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During cross-examination and in your Popovic testimony, you said that you knew that humanitarian aid was being used to feed the enemy army. Can you tell us how you obtained such intelligence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, part of the information that pertained to the work of our sector was occasionally received by Colonel Djurdjic from intelligence organs. They, in turn, had received such information either through interviews with those who crossed -- had crossed the lines or by electronic means. In other words, that information was credible and we were basically told that we were not going about our job right if such things were allowed to cross to the other side. There was information in circulation that the humanitarian assistance which was supposed to go for civilian purposes was being used to feed the Muslim army specifically in Srebrenica in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at 1D7319. Please zoom in for lieutenant-colonel. It's a document of the 25th of May, 1994. Command of the 8th Operational Group Srebrenica is reporting on how much food they had received per item. Can we go to the next page. Please zoom in. I'll read it out. "Explanation. All items of liquids are provided from humanitarian aid based on the quantities available to us."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "All items of food are provided."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Members of the armed forces are fed only when they are engaged." According to your knowledge, in May 1994 as regards the demilitarisation agreement, were such forces supposed to have been engaged?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, under the demilitarisation agreement these forces should first have been disarmed and in no case were they supposed to have been engaged, which on the other hand happened frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3307, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next can we have 1D2777 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we still have in document on the screen we see the date is the 25th of May, 1994, and now we'll see what things were like in March 1995. This cannot be the document. 1D7277. It is incorrect in the transcript. It was a proposed associated exhibit and then it was asked to be led live if necessary. This is the document. The 31st of March, 1995. It reads: "We forward an overview of the amount of food, materiel, and technical equipment and fuel issued to the military units in our area for the month of March, 18 tonnes of flour, 6 tonnes of beans, table salt, sugar, cooking oil, cans, powdered milk, and 70 litres of fuel. "We add that the above quantities were allotted from a consignment of humanitarian aid which arrived in this area through the UNHCR and this is the only source of supply of their army." How does this fit into what you and the Main Staff knew with regard to abusing humanitarian assistance at the time when they were claiming they had insufficient quantities for the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, obviously they counted their soldiers within the population since they were doing such things. We knew about that, and when they were supplied with fuel and other means then, in turn, they were capable of executing combat operation and excursions aimed at villages where they committed crimes against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have in mind the VRS or the civilians in those villages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: They had incursions where they targeted civilians for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3308, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it known in the Main Staff what my position was with regard to humanitarian assistance and were some of my orders, directives, and documents received in that regard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, orders came from you with your signature, stating that certain convoys or, as you particularly stressed, the organisation Physicians Without Borders, be let through into the enclaves or out of the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next see 18956. There is no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we'll ask you to confirm what I'm about to read out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Karadzic needs to read slowly as there is no translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is dated the 14th of May, 1993. The first line: "Pursuant to the directive of the president of Republika Srpska, strictly confidential number 01-87-1/93 of the 14th of May, 1993," that is to say the same day, "and with the aim of keeping the truce, I order the following: "Enable unhindered passage and protection of consignment, equipment, and personnel that are assisting or providing assistance to civilians on the other side. "2. Forbid abuse in military -- for military purposes the articles of food, harvest, and water-supply as well as water reserves and dams at hydro systems. "3. Abide by all regulations of the Geneva Conventions for the protection of victims of wars and their Protocols I and II as well as The Hague conventions on the laws and customs of war, et cetera. "4. Make sure that all units and the entire personnel of the army be familiarised and adhere by this order." How does this tally with regard to your knowledge of my position and the activities of the Main Staff concerning activities in the field?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, your position was clear. There are written documents in existence which I saw at the Main Staff which deal with respecting the Geneva Conventions, their Protocols, as well as The Hague Convention. And, in particular, you were adamant about treating civilians in combat areas appropriately so as to avoid, or rather, to have them extracted from the combat zone so as to avoid any casualties due to such combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It is the same document but sent as a telegraph, which is 1D7324 and that one has been translated. I wanted to tender at least the translation under that number. In any case, I seek to tender this document under whatever number or form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for marked for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3309, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D7324 is the same document in the form of a telegram. It does have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a look.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it. The same number, 420, 14 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, since the two documents are identical in terms of content, I don't see why Dr. Karadzic doesn't simply tender the one that he's just shown to us. There's no point in having two identical documents on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably received by different unit. Are you happy with tendering this one? Yes, this will be admitted as Exhibit D3309.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm waiting for the interpretation to have finished. It doesn't really matter what the form will be. This is a form which hasn't been translated, whether the telegram has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the previous one was received -- seems to have been received by the internal organ in the Main Staff. So it was not Telexed. That seems to be the reason. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have also mentioned that there were other orders, my orders, with this regard in addition to this directive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. When it comes to the 1st Krajina Corps based on those directives and orders, they organised training for those members of the Army of Republika Srpska who were in command of the units and were less familiar with the international law of war. That training was carried out by the International Committee of the Red Cross who had a lot of experience with such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at 18965. You mentioned that there were differences when it came to the supply of the United Nations forces as opposed to the aid of the civilians on the opposing side. The procedure was somewhat different. I don't think that this is it. Possibly it is. I don't know. Yes, it is. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In April 1994, as you can see here, they are quoting my order. It says here: "Based on the order of the president of Republika Srpska regarding the request of the UNPROFOR command to allow the passage of a convoy carrying supplies for the Ukrainian company in Zepa ..." and the order follows. You testified to that effect and you said that there was a difference in terms of those who were in charge of supplying the army as opposed to the others who supplied the civilians on the other side. Could you please summarise it for the Trial Chamber and tell the Trial Chamber who was in charge of what.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, UNHCR was a body that was in charge of supplying the civilian population on an exclusive basis. The UNPROFOR command was supposed to secure provisions only for its units. Those two organisations were officially separated. The UNPROFOR forces in protected zones had their own supply system. However, in practice they co-operated closely, they were closely linked. What the UNHCR did, what that organisation transported, and what it distributed and to whom in the enclave was assisted by and was well-known to UNPROFOR. The Army of Republika Srpska did not have an official insight into what was being given to whom from any of the UNHCR convoys. The only information the army had was obtained through intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is this document related to what Mr. Kralj just said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is linked with my question. I asked the witness to tell us whether there was some individual orders of mine in addition to the 1993 directives. This is another document. It's an order that is referred to in the preamble and it concerns the supplies delivered to UNPROFOR, not to the civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Edgerton, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3310, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could the army always implement its orders to lower-ranking units? Did it sometimes occur that it was not satisfied with the performance of its lower-ranking units?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, you know very well that it is not possible to implement everything with a hundred per cent success. There is always room for improvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then look at 1D5325. Please look at the document which was issued on the 29th January 1994. The Main Staff reprimands the Drina Corps and the Sarajevo Corps for not carrying out orders and irresponsible conduct vis-a-vis the Main Staff, especially when it comes to the passage of convoys. Am I right? It says here any subsequent attempt to give reasons or justifications is basically an incapacity to carry out given orders and instructions. In this regard we regard you that such and similar neglect of duty must not be repeated. How does this tally with what you know about the activities of the Main Staff, what it wanted to do, and whether it was always doable?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Main Staff insisted on full attention being paid to the safe passage of those convoys. It insisted on the convoys being escorted for their own safety in order to prevent incidents which could eventually lead to grave consequences in our co-operation with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know of such warnings to lower-ranking units? Did you know that they were warned that they should implement fully the orders issued to them by the Main Staff? Did the Main Staff make excuses for neglect and non-implementation of tasks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: No, the Main Staff did not forgive anybody, especially the Chief of Staff General Milovanovic who was very strict towards lower-ranking units, towards the subordinated units, which did not pay due attention to this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3311, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to note with regard to these documents, I've been checking as we go along and we've looked at documents from 1992 right through now to January 1994, and I note the witness has already provided evidence that he joined the Main Staff only in November 1994, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I believe that the witness told us that he was involved with convoys from 1992, first as a member of the 1st Krajina Corps and then of the Main Staff. He either sent documents of this nature or received them. Actually, it was the Main Staff who sent such documents and people in the field received them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last question about this document. Can you remember or do you know, actually, what was the position towards the United Nations personnel which escorted the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, since you are not giving evidence yourself, when you said something you need to confirm with the witness. I don't think witness either sent this document or received this one. Mr. Kralj, did you send or receive this document which you are seeing in front of you? It was sent by the Main Staff to the Drina Corps on 29th of January, 1994. It was not sent to the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, maybe I may be allowed to explain. I did not have in mind this particular document, but this type of documents that reflect the policies of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but you said in your statement at line 20 on previous page "he either sent documents of this nature or received them, documents of this nature." Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the position towards the escorts and the personal belongings of those who escorted the convoys? Did the Main Staff have a position with this regard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, the personnel who participated in the control of convoys or any kind of co-operation with UNPROFOR members were extremely fair towards the UNPROFOR or UNHCR personnel. The convoy personnel also carried equipment that was not essential to them, such as video cameras, cameras, large quantities of coffee, sugar, or equipment such as binoculars. They were kindly told that such equipment or items should not be transported and if that happened again, such equipment and items were seized from them and then there were negotiations at a higher level with representatives of UNPROFOR and UNHCR on their side and Colonel Djordjevic [as interpreted] on our side. They had their check-point or communications hub in Pale and that's where such incidents were dealt with. However, despite all that it was a commonplace occurrence that such equipment and items were transported in those convoys. The personnel of the Army of Republika Srpska was hand-picked for such tasks. Efforts were made to make sure that they did not tarnish the reputation of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D7318. 1D7318. Yes, this is the document. Zoom in, can you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here - and the document was issued on the 9th of September, 1993 - it says: "On the basis of reports from subordinate commands regarding the problems which are developing in the event of inspection of UNPROFOR teams and convoys and linked with new aspects of the political situation: "I hereby order ..." Under 1 it says: "Until further notice, do not inspect the personal belongings of personnel in UNPROFOR teams or convoys by opening back-packs or kitbags. Do a visual check and gauge the approximate weight ..." And there are some other bullet points as you can see. The last, the seventh, says: "Everything in connection with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisation has to be carried out with a lot of responsibility to avoid any possible consequences for the Republika Srpska based on the decision of the Security Council ...," and so on and so forth. Does this sound familiar to you, the fact that they gave up on controlling personal belongings of the convoy escorts? Were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I should apologise for my inertia, but Dr. Karadzic with respect to these documents continued to do which I requested he not do early on in the proceedings today, which is read a paragraph to the witness and ask him if this corresponds to what he knows or experiences, effectively leading the witness to the answer. And now Dr. Karadzic has just read a portion of the document saying: Does this sound familiar to you? In my submission, Your Honour, that's a leading question which affects the weight of the witness's answer when Dr. Karadzic, by reformulating his question - and perhaps now with respect to this document, yet again it's too late - could have a much more meaningful answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
