utterances.text: Did he not ask about the personal belongings, page 45 -- it's a separate matter whether that's a separate -- sufficient question for a foundational purpose. I think he tried to lead some foundation. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please answer, can you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, you're absolutely right. On line 20, or rather, lines 17 through 19 on page 45 I directed my interest towards the treatment of the escorts and their personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, let me tell you that I'm familiar with this document. At that time I was a member of the 1st Krajina Corps. Some check-points had their own interests and they organised their petty checks of the personal belongings of some individuals before this document was issued. In order to avoid such situations, this document was issued. If a person had their personal belongings, their toiletries, and so on and so forth, that bothered nobody. This decision was carried out and their personal belongings were from then on not searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the heading and tell us who the document was sent to. Was the 1st Krajina Corps among those units to which this order was sent?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is what it exactly says here, the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the IBK, the Herzegovina Corps, and this last bit is a bit illegible, so it's to all the corps, the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, at this point in time I have no further questions and I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3312, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just a couple of very quick background questions that I'm still not clear on. Dr. Karadzic has already mentioned - and it appears in your written evidence - that you were promoted to the rank of lieutenant-colonel in 1995. Now, as far as I understand, it's correct, isn't it, that you remained in the VRS Main Staff through 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And are you now retired from the army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Now I am a colonel, a retired colonel, or a brigadier from 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So after 1995 you were promoted again? That was what I was interested in finding out about.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I was promoted to the rank of colonel in 2002, and then I was serving in the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now just another quick question. During the time you were in the VRS Main Staff, and in particular from November 1994 till November 1995, where were you physically located?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The question is a bit unclear. Do you mean where the bed was or where I was?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where did you and Colonel Djurdjic work from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The work-place was in the command of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where precisely?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: It was called Crna Rijeka, not far away from Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your evidence today to Dr. Karadzic you said at page 30 that the VRS Main Staff wanted to avoid incidents with UNPROFOR and international organisations and that was with respect to convoy movement. You said then Muslim forces carried out propaganda activities and wanted incidents to happen, which to a large extent would lead to NATO intervention. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. When you say that, does that mean that convoys were freely allowed into Srebrenica throughout 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Convoys could enter freely unless there were some military restrictions that would prevent them from passing safely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Then by that remark about Muslim forces carrying out propaganda activities, does that also mean that UNHCR was able to meet its targets for feeding the civilian population in Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The UNHCR carried out their tasks, that is to say primarily they carried out the task of feeding the civilian population. That was its mandate; however, the problem was that part of this aid was being given to the army, the Muslim army in the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you saying it's the Muslims' fault that UNHCR was not able to meet its targets for feeding the civilian population in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: It is clear to one and all. If there is a certain quantity of food for the civilian population and more than one-third is given to the military, that is what the civilians would then lack.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So that's what you're saying, isn't it, that it's their fault?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: To a considerable degree their fault.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this isn't the first time you've appeared here in front of this Tribunal, it's actually the third, isn't it? In 2012 you appeared as a Defence witness in the Tolimir case; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you've discussed the humanitarian situation in the Srebrenica enclave in 1995 quite a bit in front of this Tribunal, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed this in detail and I answered the questions that were put to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, today in your evidence what we've seen is that with respect to convoys you were actually very well informed; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I was pretty well informed in respect of the procedure of convoy movement and documents that were in the office of Colonel Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You knew what was going in; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: In that Main Staff I was a translator and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, now, Mr. Djurdjic [sic], that was an easy question, wasn't it? It was a yes or no question. You knew what was going in and I've based that question on the evidence you've given to Dr. Karadzic today. You knew what was going in, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I had insight into documentation and from time to time I knew what went out and what came in, but I wasn't following that subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You knew how much was going as well, because you gave evidence about that in the Popovic case which has been received by this Chamber today; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Information was presented to me by the Prosecutor as to what came in, what was planned, and so on. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Because that's also what you've told Dr. Karadzic today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll move on. You knew where it went; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I knew what was written in the document regarding the movement of the convoy, and then I said that we had information about the distribution, namely, that part of the aid went to soldiers too, Muslim soldiers in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. You knew how it was used?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Food is being used for eating, and other things that are military are used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you would agree then, wouldn't you, based on everything you knew that restrictions on the delivery of humanitarian aid to Srebrenica had a debilitating effect on the civilian population there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid cannot be detrimental to the civilian population; it was welcomed by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question because you didn't seem to understand it. My question was: Based on everything you knew - and you've talked about what you knew in a great amount of detail today and in the Popovic case - based on everything you knew, you would agree, wouldn't you, that restrictions on the delivery of humanitarian aid to the Srebrenica enclave had a debilitating effect on the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. I just said that the army, the Muslim army, they took whatever they took from the convoy and they, thereby, had a debilitating effect on the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So concerted -- actually, I'll move on. Leaving that aside for a second, let's talk about the situation for Dutch UN troops in Srebrenica. You don't deny, do you, that restrictions on troop relief, troop rotation, and troop supply substantially degraded the operational effectiveness of the Dutch UN troops in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I would not agree with you in this part. Colonel Djurdjic had precise information as to what was needed and what the quantities were that the Dutch -- that the Danish [as interpreted] battalion needed for meeting their needs, fuel, ammunition, what they needed in order to perform their function.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's look at some of the evidence then that this Chamber has received and you've previously seen in your testimony in the Tolimir case. And before I call up a document I'd like to ask you this: Does having food or is having food to eat essential to the operational effectiveness of any armed force, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, in P2478, an UNPROFOR weekly situation report for the period of 26 February to 4 March 1995 -- and we can have a look at it if you want but I'll tell you what the document says, at page 5 of the English, paragraph 15, and page 6, B/C/S, we see that the UNPROFOR troops in Srebrenica literally on the 3rd of March ran out of food. And as a result, or, on that date, the Bosnian Serb army finally agreed after several prior refusals to allow the troops' resupply. So contrary -- just a moment. I'll have a -- let's leave the document off to avoid confusing the witness. Contrary to what you've just said, it doesn't appear that Colonel Djurdjic was allowing enough food for the Dutch troops to carry out their business. In fact, it doesn't even appear he was allowing sufficient food in for them to be able to survive in the enclave. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I have to tell you Colonel Djurdjic is no longer with us, but he did his job responsibly and he had exact norms that made it possible for the Dutch Battalion to carry out its tasks as far as food was concerned over a certain amount of time, and they also gave part of their food to the Muslims and that's why they didn't have enough but they didn't want to admit it. Had they said honestly: We've given this much and that's how much we lacked now, it would have been resolved quickly, urgently, knowing Colonel Djurdjic. So according to his information, they had enough food. They gave Muslims food and then they didn't have enough, and then they clamour saying that they did not have enough food, that Srebrenica did not have enough food, so that this could be looked at at a higher level, if I can put it that way, not to say intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your evidence is that DutchBat were starving themselves?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: That's not what I'm saying. I'm saying that the Dutch Battalion gave part of their food reserves to the Muslims and then it happened that for some reason they did not get enough food for themselves at a given point in time. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As a career soldier and an officer, surely you would agree with me if I was to say that fuel to run your vehicles, to keep you warm, to run electricity, fuel is essential to military troops to carry out their mission; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Fuel has its function in the army. It is true that it is of crucial importance for carrying out a mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence that from January 1995 when fuel stocks were very low, the Dutch Battalion wasn't able to heat, they weren't able to cook, they had to do everything on foot, even resupplying their observation posts. They would use occasionally local ponies to bring stuff to the observation post. Does this sound to you, Mr. Kralj, like the DutchBat had sufficient fuel to carry out their mission? And that's the evidence of Mr. Franken, T 23067 to 23068.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I'm not challenging this, but I'm challenging the period concerned because they did have enough fuel for a certain period of time. However, they had a shortage of fuel before that time expired. What happened to that fuel? They don't say that they gave it someone else here, and our norms that Milos Djurdjic had that this fuel was sufficient for them for another few days.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Kralj, the few days was far, far longer. By the 11th of July, 1995, DutchBat was unable to help the stream of refugees coming into the compound at Potocari. The food situation was hopeless. There was wounded, and DutchBat was unable to help the wounded because their supplies had not been coming in since the end of April. And that is from P00841, an UNMO report from Srebrenica dated 11 July 1995 at 1601. So, Mr. Kralj, in fact the length and the progression, the organisation of this denial of resupply suggests that it was actually systematic, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I did not know about that, that this was something that was being done systematically.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you now saying that Colonel Djurdjic didn't keep you as informed as you've given evidence to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjic informed me to the extent to which it was necessary for me to deal with the documents that had to do with UNPROFOR movement or UNHCR movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just in regard to the information that you received from Colonel Djurdjic and the extent to which it was necessary, I'd like to recall your testimony in the Tolimir trial to you and that's been uploaded as 65 ter number 24884. At page 18429 you discussed with my colleague Mr. Vanderpuye the intelligence you had about what was going on with the convoys on the ground in 1995. You said, as regards Mr. Djurdjic, that he would always briefly tell you what was going on. On the same page and over to 18430, you also explained that Djurdjic occasionally acted as the duty team leader and, as such, he was privy to everything that was going on when he was on duty. He received regular reports from his units concerning intelligence work and it was part of regular combat reporting. You also said at transcript page 18283 that Djurdjic informed you of the intentions of UNPROFOR. He received information and was in constant contact with the units that conducted checks at check-points and also the duty officer of the UNPROFOR Main Staff received reports from units about UNPROFOR activities. That was supplementary information that was included in such reports, but you paid special attention to it. Colonel Djurdjic, you said at transcript page 18393, had the necessary information about the population in the enclave and UNPROFOR presence. He also had information about the quantities of goods delivered to the enclaves in any given period. Based on all this, Mr. Kralj, I would suggest to you that you were much better informed than you've just tried to assert.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Partially you're right. I said everything that was stated there. However, I only received information that had to do with my work. I had an opportunity to look up a document if I needed it, but I didn't need much because my foremost duty was translator. I only needed what was necessary for the job. I did take part in most of the meetings, talks, and negotiations, but the frequency of convoys was rather high and I was only assigned to assist Djurdjic. I wasn't much interested in knowing about it all. What I learned I learned from documents and Djurdjic only briefly told me: Yes or no. And from that point on I didn't pay much heed to what was going on further.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've given detailed information today about the position of the Main Staff on critical issues from 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995. You've also given information today reflecting knowledge of the situation as reported from different brigades, the Rogatica Brigade and the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. You've given information reflective of Dr. Karadzic's position on critical issues or issues that he's broached with you in your examination-in-chief. Is your evidence now that you learned everything that you told us today from documents?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I state that I am familiar with what I said today either because I saw a document or I was told something by Colonel Djurdjic. As for the documents I saw while working in the 1st Corps, of course I saw such documents which were arriving in the 1st Corps in 1993 or 1994. I was the one receiving documents for implementation. The issue of convoys is something I was aware of, but I did not go into any particular detail as to what was going on in Srebrenica. I was busy with other tasks. Colonel Milos knew far more and he didn't have much time to explain to me how and what needed to be done. He only provided me with as so much information as was needed when I had to stand in.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So information about the situation for over 40.000 civilians and by July 1995 150 DutchBat personnel was information that Djurdjic did not provide you with in the event you had to stand in. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm saying. I only received information that had to do with the passage of convoys and how it was supposed to deal with it technically, who was supposed to sign what document. There was some helicopter missions that I was completely unaware of. So in a way he introduced me to that work. You must realise that I arrived in late 1994. I was engaged in translation, and when Djurdjic was away then I had to do that part of job too. We were simply short of men. Certain documents had to be sent in the pipeline and I strove to learn as much of the administrative side of things as I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your section, your sector, had no concern in assessing convoy passage requests for the needs of 40.000 civilians in the Srebrenica pocket; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I knew how many UNPROFOR personnel there were. I had no clue how many civilians there were in Srebrenica, nor did I take part in any assessments or estimates of what was needed and how much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if you knew how many UNPROFOR personnel there were, you would have known then, Mr. Kralj, that because of refusals to allow troop rotation and troop replacement, refusals that were issued from your sector, the number of personnel dropped from over 300 to just over 150 in July 1995, wouldn't you have? 147 actually.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of such information. I only learned of it here during proceedings. I knew that the total number of men in the battalion was around 300. That's all I know. Now, what UNPROFOR policy was in terms of how many people they wanted to retain and how many to rotate, that's not something that was part of my job. It was Djurdjic's job.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at something that comes out of your sector, actually, if we're talking about your job, and I'll do this very quickly before we break. Could we have a look at P4454, please. It's a document from the VRS Main Staff to the Drina Corps command dated 3 July 1995. Now, if we just look at the ordinal number at the top left corner of this page it has the prefix 06. That's your sector, isn't it? Is that your sector, 06, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- thank you. The very first paragraph of this document says that the VRS has approved convoy movement of DutchBat from Srebrenica to Zagreb the next day but has not approved the return convoy. So this is correspondence from your sector communicating a refusal for troop rotation that's specifically geared to diminish DutchBat in the Srebrenica enclave. Now, you saw the documents - you've just given that evidence - are you saying that by July 1995 you were unaware of the practice of the VRS Main Staff to reduce UN troop numbers in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I was not aware of it. I know of the document and I know that the document went in or went out and was whether approved -- was either approved or not approved.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time. I wonder if you'd like to take a lunch break now and I can conclude shortly after we return?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think probably half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break now and resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Your Honours, I've had a look at the transcript and I've been able to revise my estimate substantially.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, you might be pleased to know that having had a look at the answers you've given to my questions I have nothing further to ask of you today.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No translation, but fortunately Mr. Kralj understands English, speaking English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, several. I would just like to take the opportunity that we have this document and I would ask interpreters are they in their own cabin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, they are all in their booths. What is your point, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I don't hear any Serbian translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh. Mr. Kralj, do you hear me in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But do you hear me in B/C/S language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yeah, now, from that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, I apologise I was unaware of the rank you received from the ministry. Please look at this document and the date when a convoy that had not been approved was supposed to come back. It was on the 5th of July, 1992. It was supposed to go to Srebrenica. Can you tell the Chamber what could have been the possible reason for it, or rather, what was going on as of July 6th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, the witness has already answered that he wasn't aware of it and that's at page 60, line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I won't ask about the document then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when combat operations around Srebrenica began and would you allow anyone through a combat zone to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, we, or rather, I would not allow -- the Main Staff would not allow the passage of any convoy if there are combat activities underway or if there is a risk of the convoy sustaining damage or if its safe passage could not be secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 55 of today's transcript you were asked something about fuel. Can you tell us how combat vehicles and tanks belonging to the 28th Division, Oric's division, obtained fuel? The line in question is 1 through 19, page 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer the question, Mr. Kralj. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not disputing at all the fact that we talked about fuel, but anything related to the 28th Division was not a subject of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness answered that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had fuel in the enclave, but I'll reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this page, Colonel, it was suggested to you that perhaps your assertion is that the Dutch Battalion was starving themselves and making themselves short of fuel, and you said at another place that Colonel Djurdjic did have assessments. Can you tell us how a unit assessment is made? What did Djurdjic do in that regard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, Colonel Djurdjic was a logistics officer. He had come from the logistics organs of the Main Staff. He received from those organs information in terms of how much fuel is needed per each type of vehicle in order to have a full combat set and what the consumption of individual vehicles was. He also knew the size of the territory and what kind of tasks had to be performed. On a more senior level, he had discussions about weekly supply for the UNPROFOR forces in Srebrenica. So it wasn't something that was reduced; it was based on the norms used by both the VRS and -- well, a vehicle is a vehicle. It can only use so much fuel per kilometre. It's not something he did off the top of his head. He used norms. The same goes for food. He knew precisely what the norm was per soldier in terms of water, food, or other necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your answer you say that Colonel Djurdjic's calculations were to the effect that they had enough unless they gave it to someone and you did say that you had information that they were providing things for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Just before that let me ask you this: It was suggested to you that you were not aware of everything perhaps. Was anything kept hidden from you in the sector?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but Dr. Karadzic has just given evidence and I'm just wondering what he bases that on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was merely laying a foundation to be able to show a document and I reiterated the witness's words. Also my esteemed colleague Ms. Edgerton suggested that he may not have been aware of everything Djurdjic was, and Colonel said that Djurdjic informed him as to the part of work he did -- he had to do. And now I was asking him whether anything was kept hidden from him and I was about to follow it up with the specific items and quantities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there was no need to hide anything from me or to inform me of anything that was unimportant to my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D5105. The reference in the transcript is page 55, lines 1 through 19. Franken's words were quoted to you - he was the DutchBat colonel - to the effect that they did not have fuel and food. Let's look at this document. Please zoom in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It a Muslim document of the 5th of June, 1995. They're reporting to their command in Tuzla, that is to say the 2nd Corps, that they had received in May almost 30 tonnes of flour, 596 kilo of sugar, 1.4 tonnes of cooking oil, 5 tonnes of cold cuts, and so on and so forth --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is re-direct. Dr. Karadzic can't lead and he's leading by reading the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can ask the witness because he was asked, he was told that Franken said that they didn't have it. The witness said that it is not correct that they didn't have it. The witness perhaps can tell us what this document has to tell us and how the document tallies with what he knows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But by now you should know how to put your question in your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until my next trial I'll probably learn or until the next war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, what is this document about? I would especially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any difference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the Colonel's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your answer is this: [In English] "... I'm challenging the period concerned because they did have enough fuel for a certain period of time. However, they had a shortage of fuel before that time expired. What happened to that fuel? They don't say that they gave it someone else here, and our norms that Milos Djurdjic had that this fuel was sufficient for them for another few days." [Interpretation] On that same page you said this about food. [In English] "That's not what I'm saying. I'm saying that the Dutch Battalion gave part of the food reserves to the Muslims, and then it happened that for some reasons they did not get enough food for themselves at a given point of time. That's what I am saying." [Interpretation] Now I'm asking you: How does this document tally with what you know and what you stated earlier today? Please pay attention to the purchase of 171 litres of oil, engine oil, I believe that there was even a bigger quantity of oil purchased.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness has said in cross-examination: "What I learned I learned from documents and Djurdjic only briefly told me. From that point on I didn't pay much heed to what was going on further ..." So I don't think that this question related to this document is anything that arises from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Transcript page, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, page 58, line 23 to line 25. Actually, line 20 -- page 57, line 20 to 25, apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the -- and page numbers of the passage you referred to, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 55, lines 11 through 19, and the same page has this food reference and I would kindly ask Mr. Robinson to reply to Ms. Edgerton's intervention because it was a procedural issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the answer witness gave, we will allow the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you familiarised yourself with the document that is now on the screen in front of you, Colonel, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I'm quite familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how this tally with what you knew about the shortages in the enclave of Srebrenica? You were asked about that on the pages that have just been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, this fully corresponds with what I stated and that was that some of the assets of the Dutch Battalion was given to the Muslim army or the 28th Division and that was the official title of the division that was deployed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3226, Your Honours -- sorry, 3286.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 53 you were suggested that there were over 40.000 civilians in Srebrenica and you said that you were not fully aware of the population count. I don't know how to put the following question. However, the Trial Chamber has admitted a document according to which there were 37.000 people but they say that there were 45.000 people. Were you aware of the fact that they tried to present an unrealistic number of the population in those two enclaves and why was that done?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness -- if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness has already said at page 58 line 10: "I had no clue how many civilians there were in Srebrenica nor did I take part in any assessments or estimates of what was needed and how much." I don't think this is a question for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, but, I did not ask how many. I asked him whether there were accurate reports about the population number. Did the Muslim side present the population count accurately? Did the Main Staff know whether the number that was presented was correct or incorrect? I did not ask about the actual population count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know, or rather, you mentioned, or rather, you said that the issue of fuel was distorted due to the black market dealings and so on and so forth. Did you know about the illegal dealings in Srebrenica? Did you know about the crime there and other such things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there, were there, were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there was no mention of black markets in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or where did he say distortion in the distribution of fuel?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I haven't found that yet, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was asked, the witness was asked how it was possible or whether UNPROFOR and primarily UNPROFOR, did they choose to go starving, did they choose to lack fuel, was the population starved by the Serbs. I'm asking the witness whether there was any crime going on there. Were they aware of other forms of crime that had to do with the overall supplies of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think that question arose from the line of cross-examination. It talked about assessment of Mr. Djurdjic. I will consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is unanimous. Please move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's pay attention to page 51, line 1 to line 4. Let's see how to deal with that. Now we have it, yes: [In English] "Q. Are you saying it is the Muslims' fault that UNHCR was not able to meet its targets for feeding the civilian population in the enclave? "A. It is clear to one and all. If there is a certain quantity of food for the civilian population and more than one-third is given to the military, that is what the civilians would then lack. "Q. So that's what you are saying, isn't it, that it's their fault? "A. To a considerable degree their fault." [Interpretation] I wanted to offer a Muslim document to show you what they established through their own investigations, not what the Serbian MUP established but what the Muslim MUP did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I put a question based on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let us see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D29076 is the next document I would like to call up. I'm afraid that the translation is still pending. We will ask the Colonel to comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, would you please read from the top to the name "Naser Oric" and thus to present the Trial Chamber the contents of the document. Can you do it slowly, please? Can you do it aloud?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not an appropriate way to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we collapse the document for the moment. Without reading out or let the witness read the document, could you not put the question first?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I thought I did based on what was already answered. My question is this: Did you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- how food shortages came about to be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What witness said in his cross-examination is one-third of convoys was allegedly given to the Muslim people, so how can a criminal activity arise from there?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, what the witness said was confirmed by the official investigations carried out by the Muslim police and that was that the shortage of fuel and foodstuffs was result of criminal activities and that there would have been enough of both based on the quantities supplied.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the -- the reason for the shortage of food was discussed in the cross-examination, the Chamber will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, did the Serbian side -- and you were asked about the responsibility and the blame for all the shortages, was the Serbian side responsible for the lack of food or, in other words, the overall problems with food and the shortages in Srebrenica? Was the Serbian army responsible for those things?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Serbian army was not responsible for shortages of food in Srebrenica. It was the black market and all those groups that sold the fuel and the foodstuffs in that area on the black market because some of the prices of some of the products went through the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did they obtain the fuel and the foodstuffs from in order to resell it on the black market?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, the area was conducive to the development of the black market. Whoever could find channels to bring something to that black market would go rich very quickly and things came from Serbia and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the humanitarian aid, did some of it end up on the black market among the criminals who resold it on the black market?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, the cheapest commodities that could sell really well came from the humanitarian aid. Its entrance channels were very easy and it could sell really well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can we see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the accused please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read slowly for the Trial Chamber and the other participants, start with the institutions and end with the name of Naser Oric. Let's first identify the drafter of this document. Aloud, slowly, can you do it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can: "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Ministry of the Interior. "State Security Service. "DS DB sector Tuzla" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, you can go a little bit faster because the interpreters seem to be managing.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: "Line work 02. "Operative JK 258. "Number 7-1484. "Date: 17 November 1995. "Reference: An overview of criminal activities and persons from Srebrenica during the period leading up to the occupation of this town."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you start with line 4 where it says "Srebrenica, we recorded ..." and so on. Let's save some time.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: "... we recorded a number of acts of crime committed by the members of the 28th Division and certain leaders of the municipal bodies of power in Srebrenica. Those criminal acts involved persons who were close to the aforementioned categories of persons who, inter alia, were also one of the links in the chain of smuggling with humanitarian aid, the resale of weapons, the smuggling of oil, and similar things. All the recorded cases to a large extent resulted in the destabilisation of relationships and a further deterioration of the security situation in the protected zone of Srebrenica. Such a situation had a major impact on the relationship between the military bodies and the civilian bodies ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now let's not go into any further detail. How does this tally with what you knew and what the Main Staff knew about the destiny of the humanitarian aid that entered the enclave?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. President, this completely tallies with the information the Main Staff had as to what was happening with the humanitarian assistance in the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3313, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Kralj, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kralj, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the next witness is Mr. Mladjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, while we're waiting for the witness to come in if I might raise a concern about translations, scheduling of witnesses for next week. I can do it at the end of the day as well, whatever's more convenient for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Some weeks ago we advised Mr. Robinson that there was an issue concerning the number of exhibits, proposed associated exhibits for Mr. Skiljevic and our concerns that they might not be submitted -- translated and submitted in sufficient time to allow the Prosecution to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We considered at that time it was already getting late but allowed for the possibility that if the translations came in very quickly that we could still be prepared. As of last night there were still nearly 100 pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Mladjenovic, please wait -- please be seated and wait for a while. Thank you for your patience. Yes, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I was indicating, as of last night, the problem still persisted to a very significant extent, so much so that I raised the issue with Mr. Robinson and told him that we considered it would be next to impossible to be adequately -- to be in a position to adequately prepare for cross-examination on Monday. I am now advised that about roughly half of those documents have translations that -- but, as I mentioned before they were not uploaded as of last night, creating a problem. In addition, we spent a great deal of time trying to sort out this problem in order to get on top of it. So that was -- cost us additional time. Now we'll be in a position to try to absorb, again at the last minute, the materials that have just been made available. In addition, there are still, as I understand it, in excess of 40 pages of proposed associated exhibits for which there are no translations. This has been a continuing problem and so I raise it with the Court for that reason, even beyond the specific scheduling concern that we have. So as the -- now Mr. Robinson acknowledged when we spoke at the lunch break that there was such a problem and repeated, as he has in the past, his acknowledgement that when such problems arise that witnesses should be -- or at least the cross-examination of those witnesses should be deferred so that the Prosecution can have sufficient time to prepare. As the Court is aware, in similar circumstances we have tried our utmost to ensure that these difficulties did not result in scheduling disruptions. Nevertheless, these continuing problems cannot be cost-free. There are effects not only on the preparation of that particular witness but it simply will not continually be the case that moving the next witness forward will always suffice because there will be instances, I am sure, where moving a witness unexpectedly forward for this reason will not allow sufficient time for that witness's preparation. So I raise it. I, as always, will encourage the Prosecution team which has been extraordinary I think in meeting the challenges faced by these translation problems to deal with it as they can, but I am particularly concerned about this instance as well as the continuing problem. Finally I wanted to raise one unrelated problem to this and that is the issue of the pending motion with respect to Mr. Cavoski. That's another matter for which we can't -- he's the expert witness with reports completely without citations, basically, and that we -- we filed a motion to exclude those reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is that still pending? Pending -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think there are any number of reasons, as our motion made clear, why those reports are deficient. But certainly the one undeniable fact about the citations that we cited would mean, I think, that he would at least have to be postponed under any circumstances. But I would encourage, if possible, the most timely response on that in case, as I anticipate, it results in a scheduling gap that the Defence could still address. So those are the two matters I wanted to raise and bring to the Court's attention. I'm sorry if it delayed the commencement of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, I want to acknowledge that the Prosecution has done a really remarkable job of coping with late translations and the switching around of scheduling. So we have no -- nothing but appreciation for that and we're ready to accommodate them in any way that they would like to be accommodated. That's reasonable. In this particular case we sent these documents for translation quite a while ago and we're been waiting ourselves for them. There appear to be four untranslated documents left for Mr. Skiljevic and if that presents a problem with the commencement of his cross-examination then we won't have any objection to that being postponed. So that's essentially all I have to say about that at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Mladjenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladjenovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before your commence your evidence, Mr. Mladjenovic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule, rule of procedure and evidence, that we have here at the International Tribunal; that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Mladjenovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We do not wish to tire out the interpreters and also --

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There seem to be two microphones that are on somewhere. Perhaps it is my headphones that are causing this. I think that there was a complaint regarding poor sound. Mr. Mladjenovic, did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D7894 in e-court, and I kindly ask the interpreters to tell us whether the sound is better now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go ahead. It was probably because of my microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I misspoke or perhaps I was misinterpreted -- ah, yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this. Do you see your statement before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: I read it and I signed it. There are a few technical points. In two places, in paragraphs 8 and 10, just two words by way of correction and the rest, I mean -- well, this must have been a typo, obviously it was a typo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll deal with that. We'll ask you to correct whatever there is to be corrected, and could the witness please be shown the last page so that he could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please be so kind as to tell us what was this in paragraph 8 --

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: And 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we take a look at paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have it -- aha. Yes, I see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: The comment as to why there were more Serbs and Montenegrins than Muslims employed in education and in the municipality and then the answer follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, could you please tell us how you'd like this sentence to read. Which sentence is it anyway?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Why there were more Serbs and Montenegrins than Muslims employed in health, education, and the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it should say "in health"?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: "In health, education, and the municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: And then the answer follows. And then before paragraph 11, line 3, this is a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please read out the sentence that we have now and tell us what you would like it to read.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: I deeply --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find that sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mladjenovic, just wait until we have the para 10, probably next page for both, and please read slow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I was deeply mistaken and I will be disappointed for the rest of my life because of the missed chances and at least the minimum chances which the locals had to find, but above all it was the European and the world's powerful individuals who were 'seirli,' as the Muslims say, when the Muslims, Croats, and Serbs were bleeding." That's what I'd like to correct. "I deeply believe, could have stopped it, and they had to do it at the very beginning of the conflict," that's what I meant. As for the rest, I believe it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So when the Muslims and Croats Serbs were bleeding in the conflict that was going on, I deeply believe they could have stopped it and they had to do it at the very beginning of the conflict; is that it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If these corrections are taken into account, does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely identical. Perhaps, perhaps I'd make briefer comments, but the essence would be absolutely correct and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the 92 ter package now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And how many associated exhibits is the Defence tendering?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're tendering two, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. McKenna. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We do -- actually, there's an English translation attached to 1D04238 which is a partial duplicate of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA

utterances.text: Where is 1D7990 referred to in the witness's statement?

utterances.text: It's paragraph 41 of the witness's statement.
