utterances.text: Can I hear from you, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're happy to have these admitted. The problem was we didn't have translations and actually, as I'm looking in my own e-court at 1D4238, I don't see a translation there. But if the Prosecution has one and they can share it with the Chamber, we would be happy to have that admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We do have a translation. I thought -- I'll look into where it is and we'll share it with the Chamber certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll admit 1D4210 and 1D7990 in addition to the statement. Shall we give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour the statement will be Exhibit D3314, and 1D4210 will be Exhibit D3315, and 1D7990 will be Exhibit D3316.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out the summary of the statement of Mr. Mladjenovic in the English language and then I would deal with the document live and I would put in another two or three questions. [In English] Radojica Mladjenovic was born on 20th of November, 1949, in Mestrevac, Foca municipality. He was the president of the Executive Committee and the chief of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Foca during 1992. Negotiations between Serbs and Muslims after the multi-party elections were difficult and long, although Radojica Mladjenovic co-operated well in this period with his Muslim colleagues in the authority. Following the situation in Focatrans company which in 1990 and 1991 was still not resolved in court, there was great tension between the Muslims and Serbs -- Muslim and Serb population. Massive rallies were held by both parties. On one occasion a large crowd of Muslims gathered outside the Municipal Assembly shouting, "Go to Serbia," to the Serbs. This was perceived as an ominous message by the Serbian population. During this period, the Patriotic League and the Green Berets were formed, which worsened and polarised the relations between Serb and Muslim population. In 1990 Senad Sahinpasic, a former deputy in the joint BH Assembly brought 1.000 rifles into Foca and distributed others in the Stari Grad municipality of Sarajevo. Radojica Mladjenovic was elected as the chairman of the Foca municipality Assembly. The Executive Committee functioned with difficulty because the Muslim members maintained many unreasonable and unfeasible policies, wasting energy and preventing constructive work. As a result, the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Foca was formed in December 1991. The Crisis Staff was formed on 3rd of April, 1991 [sic]. It was temporarily tasked with issuing decisions in the name of the Assembly. Clashes had begun by this time, but fortunately with no casualties. It was the wish of the Serbs during this time to stay living together with Muslims in a common state. The Crisis Staff never ordered or abetted any maltreatment, looting, murder, or intimidation. Some movement of civilians was restricted for the safety of the population, but the situation became increasingly chaotic. Clashes began seriously on 8 of April, 1992. Mr. Radojica Mladjenovic and some colleagues of him attempted to negotiate but this was unsuccessful. Around this time a number of Muslims were briefly brought to the Livade house [sic] including some civilians. The army suspected them of having armed the Muslim people and preparing them for the battle. In August 1992, attempts were made to provide materials for the start of the school year and to repair damage done to schools, hospitals, health centres, and homes. Production facilities were guarded and war production started in 1992 and continued throughout the war years. Those who violated military rules were brought to the KPD. Nobody from the Serbian military or civilian leadership ever ordered that any crime be committed; on the contrary, they ordered that members of all units behave in accordance with the international conventions. These instructions were passed on to military officers during army meetings. Attempts were made to prevent killings as much as possible. A mixed Serbian and Muslim commission was created to investigate such incidents which were isolated, individual cases. Certain paramilitary groups appeared during the clashes. Many were involved simply to plunder rather than to protect Serbs, as they claimed. These individuals could not be identified and both military and civilian authorities regretted their presence. On one occasion in July 1992 some drunk paramilitary members detained Radojica Mladjenovic and some others. After this the civilian authorities requested intervention to help bring the rebels to justice. Regarding Muslim paramilitaries, the civilian and military structures were aware of the Green Berets, the Black Swans, the Swallows, and many other of Muslim paramilitary groups who were armed through connections in Turkey and Croatia. The military command attempted at all times to prevent destruction and looting of property of both Muslims and Serbs. This was, however, difficult to prevent given the chaos of the situation, although the police attempted to do their job seriously and acted professionally throughout the war. Regarding the KPD, it was a civilian prison that became a military prison in war time. The Crisis Staff intervened in the prison on humanitarian grounds and provided food, toiletries, and anything else possible for the prisoners in consultations with the army and the Red Cross. [Interpretation] That's the summary. And now I'm going to ask Mr. Mladjenovic a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you meant by saying that you tried by way of agreement to ensure peace and to preserve your community with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Quite certainly. We tried mutually to act by doing whatever we could to prevent a conflict. That can be shown from various documents. Also, practically we even talked about division, a division in terms of the majority part of town or villages in the belief that local communes or villages, whatever you prefer, used to have Muslim majority populations and before that Serb populations. In order to prevent a war conflict and to have entities that would ensure that the population would not have to move from their hearths that had been their home since time immemorial, we negotiated and I personally took part in these negotiations. However, documents show that these -- well, these documents were signed by three Serbs, three Muslims, including myself and the late Lojo, very legible signatures. What the prosecution noticed - and that was quite justified - is that things were added in hand. I wrote what the obligations were on both sides. I mean, maybe it wasn't really written very nicely because I was writing on my hand. Now, was it the Crisis Staffs or the police whose obligations were to carry out these points from the agreement? Unfortunately, ultimately, although I and Mr. Lojo, the late Mr. Lojo, now he's deceased, whole-heartedly support this and our only objective was to prevent a war. Unfortunately, the Muslims obviously gave up on this, but I have to state that even after Dayton in the territory of the municipality of Foca, that is to say the pre-war municipality of Foca, there are two municipalities, Foca Ustikolina in the federal part and Foca in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us please clarify this. In line 13 you said sometimes there would be a Muslim majority and sometimes there would be a Serb majority. Did you mean that there would be a Muslim majority somewhere and a Serb majority elsewhere or was it -- I mean, I'm afraid that you spoke in an idiomatic way and that's why it wasn't interpreted as you had meant it.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me explain. For years before the conflict and before the multi-party elections in 1990, every village was a mixed village. However, what was dominant was, say, there would be more Muslims in a village or a local commune and there would be less Serbs and the other way around. What we were counting on was -- I mean in the negotiations, that they should adhere to this general request for reciprocity, namely, that we both commit ourselves to guaranteed rights for the police and police controls, police checks, everything else, because there was danger looming. Also education and many other spheres were also under a question mark. That's why I think this was mentioned in the statement. Reciprocity would be protection of both peoples with the same rights that both would enjoy in one municipality or the other. After all, that was confirmed after Dayton, that both, police, education, everything else, in Foca Ustikolina and Foca as a municipality that belongs to the Serb entity. And Foca Ustikolina in the Federation has its own police administration, an Assembly, elected Assembly, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4239, could I call that up, please. It is paragraph 23 from your statement that speaks of these agreements. Can we please take a look at this now and could you please explain this agreement to us and tell us what all of that is about. 1D4239. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, can you explain the date to us and could you tell us under which circumstances this was done and what is contained?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, what did you mention now? Was it a point? Was it a paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Twenty-three.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty-three. In my statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there's a reference to this paragraph. Can you focus on it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the screen, Mr. Mladjenovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is the agreement. I can't see any signatures. There should be signatures on one of the copies. On the left-hand side and somewhere on the right-hand side margin I added something in my own hand. This copy is identical in terms of the contents, but the original is the one where you can see signatures. Obviously there is a misunderstanding in the copying. I believe that you have both copies in your possession. They are identical. This is my handwriting in the margin. The handwriting is not very neat. I was writing standing up. And these are the obligations of all those who were present; i.e., the Crisis Staffs are mentioned as well as the police, and so on and so forth. At that time we did not call our police "policija" but "milicija," that was according to the system. I recognise the signatures, my own, Lojo's and several other signatures including the two Muslim signatures that I do not recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously they were members of the Executive Board or the leadership of the SDA, I suppose, or some other management bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was signed on the 8th of April; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were discussions before that, but that was obviously what the situation was at the time and everything pointed to a possible division that had to be carried out or delineation as it says here because otherwise bad things could happen and they did as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is more proof to that but we will come to that, won't we?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, the agreement or the document in question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the translation is similar, it's not exact. The versions of the documents are slightly different, so I would suggest that the document be marked for identification pending a proper translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's just a translation issue. Why are two versions different from each other? Is it possible to upload page 1 and page 2 separately only in B/C/S? For example, item number 2, 3 in the page 1, we have some word about "Crisis Staff" in parenthesis which we don't see on page 2. And I don't think the item number 21 is identical. I'm not sure. And whether we are seeing the identical signature or not. Can you explain that, Mr. Mladjenovic? Or, Ms. McKenna, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Perhaps it's better if Mr. Mladjenovic explains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is absolutely one and the same document. It shows various peoples' obligations. It shows who would be responsible for each of the items, who would be tasked with, for example, bullet point 21 where it says the police curfew is being introduced, and I can see it on the other papers as well. I suppose that this copy has handwritten addition and I believe that the Muslim side also made some handwritten addition when we asked for the co-operation of the police, the Crisis Staffs, and so on and so forth. So we both made our handwritten additions. This is the essence of the matter. There is nothing else. There are no other differences between the two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you take a look at item number 2. After the return of all units to their homes, on the left side it's empty but on the right side, i.e., page 1, it has the "Crisis Staff" in the parenthesis --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the implementation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So why --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my question is why there are two versions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is absolutely one and the same copy; however, one has comments in order to explain, or rather, to make a note of who would be in charge of the implementation. The same copy, the same typewriter. You have to believe me that the gist is the same. When the document was copied, the one that is on the right-hand side, the comments were cropped. I can even see a little part of my signature at the bottom of the right-hand side copy. So this is certainly, it must be the document which is relevant and which they probably also had.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we perhaps ask the witness what is the link between the handwritten annotations on the left-hand side and the remarks that are typed up on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: I personally made comments in my own handwriting. That was on the 8th of April immediately after, or rather, before the activities on the 8th of April, 1992. I suppose it was in the early hours. And I quickly jotted down while I was standing up, I jotted down what our side, our Serbian side, should do with the Muslim side because both Crisis Staffs are often mentioned as well as the police depending on the nature of the bullet point under numbers from 1 to 21.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can be more specific if we may be given the document back on the screen. Return the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about bullet points 2 and 3? Can you read the handwritten annotations on the left-hand side and can you draw a parallel with the right-hand side version?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Crisis Staff and observers if I'm not mistaken because observers were also defined as those who would supervise the implementation of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And look at the right-hand side version, do you find the word "Crisis Staff" anywhere? If you do where?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: In the right-hand side version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Bullet points 2 and 3, for example.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: The word is typed up on the right-hand side. I don't know why Crisis Staffs, both the Muslims and the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you then tell us the handwritten annotations on the one document, have they been typed up on the other document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not excluding that, but in any case every single letter of the agreement is the same in both documents. Unfortunately I don't have it here. I believe that the pencils that were used to sign the document are the same, some used a ball-point pen. They've signed the final document. This is a copy. So I would say that every bullet point is credible, it's authentic, and this is the essence of the matter. On the right-hand side you can see comments, Crisis Staff, that I added and here somebody typed it up. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mladjenovic, if you touch the screen it disappears. Shall we show him the bottom of the page on both documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see your signature on both pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the right-hand side at the top I can recognise the cropped part -- I apologise. I made the mistake again. You can discern one part of my signature on the left-hand side, and I know the other person, Tajvo. His signature is also there and the other signatures, I don't know who the other signatures are. I really don't know, believe me. And I don't know who the two Muslims, there is one person called Laki Lakovic [phoen] and Himro Rajic [phoen] on the first document, and I believe that Podrago [phoen] also signed on the Serbian side. And Asim Rajic and the other two their signatures are not legible, I can't recognise them, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that the Chamber has a basis to admit this document. We'll admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain just one more thing. You were talking about difficulties in communications between Foca and Pale. Is this your position? What were communications like between Foca and Pale during the first few months up to September 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: The communications for the first two or three days while Mr. Ostojic was in Foca were possible. After that, they were absolutely imperfect; i.e., they were non-existent. You will see from some other paragraphs that people went on foot to obtain certificates for a commissioner who was supposed to help civilian authorities in Foca and reinforce their activities. I am sorry that in September, October, and further on when we had those communications we had a fax machine on foil, and those faxes, i.e., the information that we received, faded so unfortunately none of that could be preserved as material that could be used for those purposes. I only know that some of the orders arrived and they were warnings, not so much orders. At the address of the information centre they had a printer machine that could type such documents. I received warnings from Dr. Karadzic that we should strictly adhere, or rather, that military conscripts had to adhere to Geneva Conventions and Geneva warnings so that the military structures in conversation with their soldiers, high- and low-ranking officers commented upon that and warned all of the soldiers in their units. I'm not saying that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now asking you about the document. We'll move on to other things later. In September did you meet with General Mladic and other officials? Did you attend a meeting of some kind at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: In September 1992, General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: It is quite possible. Not in Pale, that's for sure. Perhaps in Foca or thereabouts. Maybe he asked me to have a cup of coffee, somewhere there, in Bileca, but I absolutely don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber needs to rise in two or three minutes so if you have more shall we do it tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that will be enough. If we can get really quickly P1480 it will be enough. Typed-up version. P1480, typed up version, page 60. The typed-up version, typewritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Foca, 17 September, can you see that this is General Mladic's diary?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that it was Foca because Kovac is mentioned. He was the commander of the TG there. I suppose that the tactical group was in question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now go to page 67 in English and in B/C/S version. Sixty-seven in e-court. Sixty-seven in English and Serbian. We have it in English. Vojislav Maksimovic and we are waiting for the Serbian page. Here Mr. Maksimovic - he is a deputy and the member of the academia - he says that there is poor co-ordination with Cajnice, Pale and Bileca. In September was that co-ordination still poor?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct in late September up to 10 October, the joint forces of the Serbian army of Gacko and Foca suppressed from Gucevo and Zelengora mountains the Muslim forces and the army in Foca from then on controlled the entire territory of the municipality of Foca. As they were withdrawing across the Suceska river towards Gacko they blew up the bridge. The Muslims did that and it was repaired only sometime in 1994, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can we look at page 69 in English and Serbian. Let's see what you said to all that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll rise for today. Mr. Mladjenovic, can I advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. We'll continue --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 5th day of April, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.50 p.m.,
